Learning goal: You will moving in the Plane.
The purpose of this lesson is to introduce you to translations and rotations of plane figures and to have them describe these movements in everyday language. translations.title: Making the Moves
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will making the Moves.
In the previous lesson, you were introduced to the terms “translation,” “rotation,” and “reflection.” In this lesson, you understand that: - A translation is determined by two points that specify the distance and direction of the translation. - A rotation is determined by a point, angle of rotation, and a direction of rotation. - A reflection is determined by a line. These moves are called transformations for the first time and you draw images of figures under these transformations. You also study where shapes go under sequences of these transformations and identify the steps in a sequence of transformations that takes one figure to another.

- Comprehend that a “transformation” is a translation, rotation, reflection, or a combination of these
- Draw a transformation of a figure using information given orally

- Identify (orally and in writing) the features that determine a translation, rotation, or reflection
- Read the hour and minute hands separately; for hour and half-hour times, :00 and :30 must match the minute-hand position.

Learning goal: You will no Bending or Stretching.

The previous lesson examines the impact of rotations on line segments and polygons. This lesson focuses on the effects of rigid transformations on lines. In particular, you see that parallel lines are taken to parallel lines and that a \(180^\circ\) rotation about a point on the line takes the line to itself.

- Draw and label rigid transformations of a line and explain the relationship between a line and its image under the transformation
- Generalize (orally) that “vertical angles” are congruent using informal arguments about 180 degree rotations of lines
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Learning goal: You will composing Figures.
In this lesson, you create composite shapes using translations, rotations, and reflections of polygons and continue to observe that the side lengths and angle measures do not change. translations.title: What Is the Same?
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will what Is the Same?.
In this lesson, you explore what it means for shapes to be “the same” and learn that the term congruent is a mathematical way to talk about figures being the same that has a precise meaning. Specifically, you learn that two figures are congruent if there is a sequence of translations, rotations, and reflections that moves one to the other. You learn that figures that are congruent can have different orientations, but corresponding lengths and angle measures are equal.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Compare and contrast (orally and in writing) side lengths, angle measures, and areas using rigid transformations to explain why a shape is or is not congruent to another
- Comprehend that congruent figures have equal corresponding side lengths, angle measures, and areas
- Describe (orally and in writing) two figures that can be moved to one another using a sequence of rigid transformations as “congruent.”
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.

Learning goal: You will solving Any Linear Equation.
The purpose of this lesson is to move towards a general method for solving linear equations. In the warm-up, you solve equations mentally, including equations with negative coefficients, prompting a discussion of multiplying or dividing each side of an equation by a negative number. In the first activity, you encounter several different structures of equations, and take turns suggesting moves for solving them.

- Calculate a value that is a solution to a linear equation in one variable, and explain (orally) the steps used to solve
- Create an expression to represent a number puzzle, and justify (orally) that it is equivalent to another expression
- Justify (orally) that each step used in solving a linear equation maintains equality
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
